claims.label: Legal recognition
claims.statement: Château-Grillet was recognised as an appellation d'origine contrôlée by the decree of 8 December 1936, making it one of the corridor's two oldest cru recognitions; the specification in force is the one homologated by the arrêté of 4 July 2024.

claims.label: One grape, a few hectares
claims.statement: Château-Grillet is a still white wine made from Viognier alone, over roughly 3.5 hectares in the communes of Saint-Michel-sur-Rhône and Vérin in the Loire department.

claims.label: The ground
claims.statement: The specification describes sandy soils derived from primary-era granite, locally enriched with fine material beneath the château, over a fractured subsoil.

claims.label: Inside, or beside?
claims.statement: The Château-Grillet specification says the vineyard "a la particularité d'être inséré au cœur même de celui de l'appellation d'origine contrôlée « Condrieu »" — inserted into the heart of the Condrieu vineyard. The INAO product surface instead places it just south of Condrieu. Physical description and delimited geography are not the same statement, and neither makes Château-Grillet a part of Condrieu: they are independently delimited appellations.

claims.label: Appellation, estate, owner
claims.statement: Artémis Domaines records that the Pinault family acquired Château Grillet in 2011 and describes it as one of the very few French monopole AOCs and one of the smallest. The specification's own historical account describes continuous ownership by a single family line from 1830, which is a statement about the estate's past, not about its ownership today.

claims.label: Legal recognition
claims.statement: Condrieu was recognised as an appellation d'origine contrôlée by the decree of 27 April 1940; the specification in force is the one homologated by the arrêté of 4 July 2024.

claims.label: One colour, one grape
claims.statement: Condrieu is a still white wine and its specification states plainly that "les vins sont issus du cépage viognier B" — Viognier and nothing else.

claims.label: Sweetness is a range
claims.statement: The specification's own account describes a wine that was doux in the mid-nineteenth century and is in most cases sec, sometimes demi-sec, in its modern form, with confidential quantities of moelleux or doux made from overripe grapes when conditions allow. "Dry white Viognier" is therefore the usual case, not the legal definition.

claims.label: Where it is
claims.statement: The geographic area runs across seven communes and three departments: Condrieu in the Rhône; Chavanay, Malleval, Saint-Michel-sur-Rhône, Saint-Pierre-de-Bœuf and Vérin in the Loire; and Limony in the Ardèche. INAO gives the vineyard as roughly 100 hectares of terraced right-bank hillside.

claims.label: Near-disappearance and recovery
claims.statement: The specification records phylloxera devastating the vineyard in 1893, then the First World War and industrial employment draining the labour the terraces needed, until by 1965 only some eight hectares remained. It records the vineyard climbing back past 140 hectares by 2010 after a long replanting and terrace-rebuilding effort.

claims.label: Legal recognition
claims.statement: Cornas was recognised as an appellation d'origine contrôlée by the decree of 5 August 1938; the specification in force is the one homologated by the arrêté of 4 July 2024.

claims.label: One colour, one grape
claims.statement: The Cornas specification states that "les vins sont issus du cépage syrah N". Cornas is red only and admits no accessory or white variety at all — the single-variety outlier among the eight crus.

claims.label: The amphitheatre
claims.statement: The specification describes most of the vineyard as sitting on soils weathered from primary eruptive rock of the granite family — the porphyritic granites of Tournon — in an amphitheatre open to the south and sheltered from the north by the Arlettes massif, terraced behind stone walls.

claims.label: Who bottled first?
claims.statement: The Cornas specification records that the first bottling on behalf of a private cellar happened only in 1952, fourteen years after the appellation was recognised. Trade accounts variously credit Joseph Michel with pioneering domaine-bottled Cornas in 1956 and Auguste Clape with being the village's first producer to bottle his own wine in 1957. CARTA keeps the regulatory date and both attributions rather than choosing a founder.

INAO defines Cornas AOP as a red-wine appellation delimited on the sole commune of Cornas and produced only from Syrah; physical location in the commune does not by itself prove that a parcel falls within the delimited AOP.

claims.statement: Syrah is the principal variety and must be at least 80% of the holding's encépagement; Viognier is the accessory variety, permitted in mixed plantings within the Syrah parcels up to 20% of the vines. claims.label: Legal recognition
claims.statement: Crozes-Hermitage was recognised as an appellation d'origine contrôlée by the decree of 4 March 1937; the specification in force is the one homologated by the arrêté of 10 December 2024.

claims.label: Two colours, three grapes
claims.statement: Crozes-Hermitage may be red or white. Reds require Syrah to be at least 85% of the encépagement, with Marsanne and Roussanne admitted as accessory varieties in mixed plantings up to 15% of the vines; whites are Marsanne and Roussanne.

claims.label: Where it is
claims.statement: The geographic area covers eleven Drôme communes on the left bank facing Tournon — Beaumont-Monteux, Chanos-Curson, Crozes-Hermitage, Erôme, Gervans, Larnage, Pont-de-l'Isère, La Roche-de-Glun, Serves-sur-Rhône, Tain-l'Hermitage and part of Mercurol-Veaunes. It is the largest of the eight crus and the least uniform.

claims.label: Two different grounds
claims.statement: The specification splits the appellation in two. In the north the Rhône has cut down to the granite de Tournon between Crozes-Hermitage and Serves-sur-Rhône, and sandy clays and granitic arenas are held on the slopes by dry-stone terraces. In the south and east lie Quaternary terraces of alpine gravels, with loess locally at the Gervans quartier of Les Blancs and distinctive kaolin sands at Larnage.

claims.label: One commune becomes eleven
claims.statement: The 1937 decree limited the area to part of the single commune of Crozes-Hermitage; postwar prosperity and vineyard expansion took it to eleven communes by 1952. A later reselection of the parcels from which grapes may come cut the production potential from 4,800 to 3,200 hectares.

claims.label: Where geology and law disagree
claims.statement: The Crozes-Hermitage specification identifies its northern granite as the same formation that appears across the Rhône around Tournon, in Saint-Joseph. Geology crosses the river and the appellation boundary; the law does not.

The Crozes-Hermitage specification describes Les Chassis as the lowest and youngest of the Quaternary terraces, forming a triangle whose apex is at Pont-de-l'Isère and whose gravels were carried down by alpine rivers.

claims.label: Legal recognition
claims.statement: Hermitage was first recognised as an appellation d'origine by a judgment of the tribunal de Valence dated 25 June 1936 and then as an appellation d'origine contrôlée by the decree of 4 March 1937; the specification in force is the one homologated by the arrêté of 10 December 2024.

claims.label: Red, white and a third form
claims.statement: Hermitage may be red or white, and white wines may additionally carry the vin de paille mention. Reds require Syrah to be at least 85% of the encépagement with Marsanne and Roussanne as accessory varieties; whites and vin de paille come from Marsanne and Roussanne.

claims.label: Three communes, two appellations
claims.statement: The appellation covers three Drôme communes — Tain-l'Hermitage, Crozes-Hermitage and Larnage — on the left bank. The commune named Crozes-Hermitage therefore contains land in both appellations, which is exactly why a commune name cannot tell a reader which wine a parcel may make.

claims.label: What vin de paille requires
claims.statement: The vin de paille mention requires the grapes to be dried for at least 45 days between harvest and pressing, a minimum natural richness of 170 grams of sugar per litre — about 19.5% potential alcohol — and a yield of 15 hectolitres per hectare.

INAO describes the Hermitage vineyard as sitting on a fragment of granitic massif separated from the Ardèche mountains by the Rhône, with south-facing hillsides terraced behind stone walls. The hill is one landform; Hermitage AOC and Crozes-Hermitage AOC are two legal areas that meet it differently.

claims.statement: Jurançon is a Pyrenean-foothill white-wine AOP centered on Petit Manseng and Gros Manseng, with established dry and sweet traditions.

claims.label: Jurançon landscape
claims.statement: INAO describes hillside vineyards in the Pyrenean foothills under oceanic influence, with a warm dry southerly autumn wind that can support ripening and concentration.

claims.label: Dry + sweet
claims.statement: Jurançon includes dry and sweet white-wine traditions centered on Petit Manseng and Gros Manseng; sweetness is a style distinction inside the appellation, not a different geography.

claims.label: Three legal paths
claims.statement: The current Jurançon specification distinguishes three white-wine paths in the same geography: Jurançon sec at no more than 4 grams per litre of fermentable sugars, Jurançon above 40 grams per litre, and Jurançon vendanges tardives above 55 grams per litre.

claims.label: Principal + accessory grapes
claims.statement: The current Jurançon specification names Gros Manseng and Petit Manseng as principal varieties and Camaralet de Lasseube, Courbu, Lauzet and Petit Courbu as accessory varieties; the vendanges tardives mention is reserved to the two Mansengs.

claims.label: Harvest changes the path
claims.statement: All Jurançon grapes are hand harvested. Successive picking passes are required except for Jurançon sec, while vendanges tardives fruit cannot be harvested before 2 November; off-vine passerillage is prohibited apart from handling within the parcel during harvest.

claims.label: Why ripeness keeps freshness
claims.statement: Jurançon’s wet Atlantic foothills are tempered in autumn by a frequent warm, dry southerly foehn. On steep slopes and terraces, late, thick-skinned local grapes can concentrate while retaining high acidity and resisting grey rot, which helps explain how dry, sweet and late-harvest wines remain distinct paths rather than different places.

claims.label: Wine-growing communes
claims.statement: INAO describes the Jurançon production area across 25 communes between Pau and the Pyrenees.

claims.label: Member vineyards
claims.statement: The Vignerons du Jurançon association reports 620 hectares of member vineyards; this is not represented as the total AOP vineyard area.
Jurançon is a French AOP documented by INAO.

INAO describes Jurançon as hillside viticulture at the Pyrenean foothills under an oceanic climate with a frequent warm, dry southerly autumn wind; sweet wines were recognized in 1936 and dry Jurançon in 1975, with hand harvesting linked to high-trained vines and steep terrain.
INAO describes Petit Manseng and Gros Manseng as the principal local grape varieties of Jurançon.

claims.label: Legal recognition
claims.statement: Saint-Joseph was recognised as an appellation d'origine contrôlée by the decree of 15 June 1956, the last of the eight crus to be created; the specification in force is the one homologated by the arrêté of 4 July 2024.

claims.label: Two colours, three grapes
claims.statement: Saint-Joseph may be red or white. For reds the specification requires Syrah to be at least 90% of the holding's encépagement, with Marsanne and Roussanne permitted only as accessory varieties in mixed plantings within the Syrah parcels up to 10% of the vines, and wines made from both colours must be "vinifiés par assemblage des raisins concernés". Whites come from Marsanne and Roussanne.

claims.label: A corridor, not a hill
claims.statement: The geographic area covers 26 communes — 23 in the Ardèche and three in the Loire — strung over roughly sixty kilometres of right bank. One appellation name therefore covers a long sequence of different slopes rather than a single côte.

claims.label: An outline that moved twice
claims.statement: The specification records Saint-Joseph beginning in 1956 on six communes around Tournon, expanding in 1969 by twenty further communes reaching north to the Condrieu area, and then being significantly narrowed by parcel revisions approved on 9–10 February 1994 and 20 June 2018, which cut the delimited parcel area from about 6,800 to about 3,400 hectares. Today's outline is a made thing, not a timeless one.

claims.statement: Saint-Péray was recognised as an appellation d'origine contrôlée by the decree of 8 December 1936.

claims.label: Still and sparkling
claims.statement: Saint-Péray is a white-wine appellation covering both "vins blancs tranquilles" and "vins blancs mousseux", the sparkling wines made by a second fermentation in bottle, from Marsanne and Roussanne, over the communes of Saint-Péray and Toulaud in the Ardèche. INAO gives sparkling wine as roughly a tenth of the volume.

claims.label: The ground
claims.statement: The specification describes a primary granitic basement of the Massif Central, secondary limestone deposits that left the Crussol massif standing, and soils that combine calcareous, clay-limestone and granitic material where the Rhône later carved a collapse basin.

claims.label: Where the bubbles came from
claims.statement: The Saint-Péray specification traces bottle-fermentation experiments to a merchant's cellarmaster in 1730 and records Louis-Alexandre Faure conducting systematic trials on a hundred barrels in 1828, an innovation it describes as unique in the Rhône valley at the time.

claims.label: A rule change in progress
claims.statement: A modification of the Saint-Péray specification was adopted by the Comité national des appellations d'origine relatives aux vins et aux boissons alcoolisées on 6 February 2025 and placed in the national opposition procedure. A proposal in opposition is not law: CARTA records it as a dated observation and does not present it as the rule in force.

The Saint-Péray specification records Louis-Alexandre Faure carrying out systematic bottle-fermentation trials on a hundred barrels in 1828, following an earlier experiment by a merchant's cellarmaster in 1730, and treats this as the beginning of the reputation that sparkling Saint-Péray carried through the nineteenth century.

The Saint-Péray specification describes a primary-era granitic basement over which secondary deposits built a limestone massif, leaving the Crussol relief standing above the appellation, with soils that mix calcareous, clay-limestone and granitic material.

Jurançon is a Pyrenean-foothill white-wine AOP centered on Petit Manseng and Gros Manseng, with established dry and sweet traditions.

claims.label: Jurançon landscape
claims.statement: INAO describes hillside vineyards in the Pyrenean foothills under oceanic influence, with a warm dry southerly autumn wind that can support ripening and concentration.

claims.label: Dry + sweet
claims.statement: Jurançon includes dry and sweet white-wine traditions centered on Petit Manseng and Gros Manseng; sweetness is a style distinction inside the appellation, not a different geography.

claims.label: Three legal paths
claims.statement: The current Jurançon specification distinguishes three white-wine paths in the same geography: Jurançon sec at no more than 4 grams per litre of fermentable sugars, Jurançon above 40 grams per litre, and Jurançon vendanges tardives above 55 grams per litre.

claims.label: Principal + accessory grapes

claims.label: Harvest changes the path
claims.statement: All Jurançon grapes are hand harvested. Successive picking passes are required except for Jurançon sec, while vendanges tardives fruit cannot be harvested before 2 November; off-vine passerillage is prohibited apart from handling within the parcel during harvest.

claims.label: Why ripeness keeps freshness
claims.statement: Jurançon’s wet Atlantic foothills are tempered in autumn by a frequent warm, dry southerly foehn. On steep slopes and terraces, late, thick-skinned local grapes can concentrate while retaining high acidity and resisting grey rot, which helps explain how dry, sweet and late-harvest wines remain distinct paths rather than different places.

claims.label: Member vineyards

claims.label: What the region is
claims.statement: Northern Rhône is a collective name for the eight cru appellations of the Rhône corridor between Vienne and Valence — Côte-Rôtie, Condrieu, Château-Grillet, Saint-Joseph, Crozes-Hermitage, Hermitage, Cornas and Saint-Péray. Each of those eight is separately delimited by its own specification; no appellation, mention or delimited area named Northern Rhône exists, so CARTA holds the region as an editorial grouping with no legal boundary of its own.

claims.label: Which bank
claims.statement: Six of the eight crus sit on the Rhône's right, western bank — Côte-Rôtie, Condrieu, Château-Grillet, Saint-Joseph, Cornas and Saint-Péray — while Hermitage and Crozes-Hermitage sit on the left bank around Tain-l'Hermitage. Bank is an orientation fact and nothing more: it does not predict landform, substrate or permitted grape.

claims.label: Eight rulebooks, twenty years
claims.statement: The eight crus were recognised across two decades and never as one act: Château-Grillet and Saint-Péray by decrees of 8 December 1936, Crozes-Hermitage and Hermitage on 4 March 1937 (Hermitage having first been recognised as an appellation d'origine by a judgment of the tribunal de Valence on 25 June 1936), Cornas on 5 August 1938, Condrieu on 27 April 1940, Côte-Rôtie on 18 October 1940 and Saint-Joseph only on 15 June 1956. Different dates froze different rules.

claims.label: The broader legal background
claims.statement: The regional Côtes du Rhône AOP extends along the valley from the Vienne sector towards Avignon and overlaps the northern corridor. It is the legal home of fruit that the crus do not cover, which is why a vineyard can sit among the crus and still be sold under a broader name.

claims.label: Four grapes, eight settings
claims.statement: Four grapes carry the whole corridor: Syrah is the only red variety permitted in any of the five red crus, Viognier is the sole variety of Condrieu and Château-Grillet and the only white admitted into a Côte-Rôtie red, and Marsanne and Roussanne are the white pair of Saint-Joseph, Crozes-Hermitage, Hermitage and Saint-Péray. The same four varieties are re-weighted by each specification rather than by geography.

claims.label: How to read the map
claims.statement: The active outlines in this world are INAO cartographic representations of eight regulatory geographical areas. They are not vineyard land, not parcel eligibility and not a Northern Rhône polygon; the region label is a derived orientation anchor over the mapped crus.

claims.label: Cru appellations

claims.label: Legal recognition
claims.statement: Château-Grillet was recognised as an appellation d'origine contrôlée by the decree of 8 December 1936, making it one of the corridor's two oldest cru recognitions; the specification in force is the one homologated by the arrêté of 4 July 2024.

claims.label: Legal recognition

claims.statement: Full carbonic maceration begins with intact whole bunches in a closed, oxygen-excluding carbon-dioxide atmosphere, allowing intracellular metabolism in intact berries before pressing and completion of fermentation.

Semi-carbonic maceration is related to but distinct from full carbonic maceration: fermentation of juice released in a whole-bunch vat can generate carbon dioxide around intact berries, so ordinary yeast fermentation and some intracellular metabolism proceed together without requiring a fully established external-CO2 treatment.
Whole-cluster fermentation describes the inclusion of intact bunches and stems; by itself it does not establish whether a ferment is full carbonic, semi-carbonic or neither.

Four Northern Rhône specifications — Côte-Rôtie, Saint-Joseph, Crozes-Hermitage and Hermitage — require that wines made from both the red and the white permitted varieties be "vinifiés par assemblage des raisins concernés": assembled as grapes, in the same proportion, rather than blended after fermentation. The rule governs when the varieties may meet, not whether any given producer uses the white grape at all.

claims.statement: René-Jean Dard's own account gives 1983 as the first vintage he and François Ribo made together, and 1984 as the year they "began properly". CARTA keeps both: they are two different events, not one contested date.

Dard describes the estate being assembled by renting vineyards from their owners and expanding gradually across parcels in Crozes-Hermitage, Hermitage and Saint-Joseph. A single cellar point cannot stand in for that patchwork, and rented land is not owned land.

Dard describes deciding to plough rather than use herbicides from the mid-1980s, and says explicitly that what interests them is "the notion of working cleanly" rather than holding an organic certification or a logo for the label. Absence of certification here is a stated choice, not evidence of conventional farming.

Reds are described as ten to fifteen days of maceration with whole bunches — unless sunburn requires sorting, in which case a destemmer is used — fermented in large wood with the cap broken once a day and aged in 500-litre demi-muids; whites are pressed whole-bunch.

Dard told Louis/Dressner that making natural wine "should not be a goal unto itself" but "a tool to make qualitatively superior wine", and that he had made sulfur-free wines since he was fifteen, following his father. He told LITTLEWINE that their goal is not to make wine without sulfites but to make good wine, and that if a wine is going a bit wild they do not stop themselves adding some.

location.description: Dard & Ribo work from a cellar base at Mercurol while farming rented parcels across Crozes-Hermitage, Hermitage and Saint-Joseph. One base point could not stand for that patchwork even if a coordinate had been acquired; none is asserted here.

claims.statement: Skurnik records Alain Graillot returning home to Crozes-Hermitage to start his own domaine in 1985, and his sons Maxime and Antoine being in charge since 2008, with hand harvesting, organic farming, whole-cluster fermentation and ageing in one- to three-year-old barrels bought from Burgundy estates.

One estate holds both of Saint-Péray's wine forms at once: a traditional-method sparkling wine presented as the continuation of the appellation's nineteenth-century reputation, and a barrel-vinified still wine created in 1984 as a deliberate departure from what most of the appellation was then doing. The domaine also works Cornas.

Les Bulles d'Alain is 100% Marsanne, méthode traditionnelle, brut nature, with a second fermentation in bottle and four years on lattes. The estate says it perpetuates the traditional-method Saint-Péray that made the region's reputation from the 1830s.

claims.statement: The estate records the Ongrie cuvée as created in 1984, 100% Marsanne, vinified exclusively in 228- and 400-litre oak, at a time when "l'essentiel de la production de Saint-Péray était issue de la méthode traditionnelle et les vins étaient vinifiés en cuves" — most Saint-Péray was sparkling and still wines were made in tank. The estate describes Alain Voge as the precursor of barrel work in Saint-Péray.

claims.statement: The Rare Wine Co. records Auguste Clape as the village's first producer to bottle his own wine in 1957, having previously sold in barrel to négociants, with his son Pierre-Marie working alongside him from 1989 and grandson Olivier following. The domaine acquired century-old vines from Noël Verset.

Old-vine fruit is not destemmed, primary fermentation runs six to seven days in concrete, ageing uses old neutral demi-muids and pièces with no new oak, and the flagship Cornas is blended from five or six cuvées of the oldest vines. A Côtes du Rhône bottling includes fruit from 120-year-old vines near Saint-Péray together with declassified Cornas.

The Guide Hachette records the Gripa family arriving at Saint-Péray in the seventeenth century and settling at Mauves around 1850, Fabrice Gripa running the domaine since 2001 after his father Bernard, and eighteen hectares spanning Saint-Joseph and Saint-Péray with the Les Figuiers, Les Pins and Le Berceau cuvées.

claims.statement: Domaine Cauhapé describes a Monein estate on southeast-facing Jurançon slopes, with vineyards rising to about 400 metres and a range that deliberately includes both dry and sweet wines.

claims.statement: The Wine Trust describes Chambeyron-Manin's vineyard work as sustainable and using organic methods; CARTA does not treat this as evidence of formal certification.
Current importer material describes the Syrah vines as roughly 40 to more than 50 years old.
The domaine farms a single roughly 0.5-hectare parcel on Côte Brune above Ampuis; importer descriptions place it on iron-rich schist with a very steep slope and hand-worked vines.
Domaine Christiane Chambeyron-Manin is a micro-estate in Côte-Rôtie currently owned and run by Véronique Manin.
The Wine Trust identifies Christiane as Véronique Manin's mother and explains that the domaine name incorporates family names from Véronique's maternal and paternal lines.

Chambeyron-Manin's Côte-Rôtie is made from Syrah from the domaine's 0.5-hectare Côte Brune parcel; importer sources describe the parcel as planted exclusively to Syrah using the local 'Sérine' selection/clone terminology.

Sacred Thirst documents whole-cluster native-yeast fermentation in concrete tanks, basket pressing, transfer by gravity into 500-liter barrels with up to one-third new oak depending on vintage, and about 18 months of élevage before unfined, unfiltered bottling.

location.description: Importer sources place the domaine's roughly 0.5-hectare Syrah parcel on Côte Brune above Ampuis. Exact parcel geometry remains unresolved.

claims.statement: Domaine de la Grand’Cour states that Jean Dutraive acquired the estate in 1969 with nine hectares in Fleurie across Grand’Cour, Chapelle des Bois and Champagne; Jean-Louis Dutraive joined in 1977 and succeeded him in 1989.

Domaine de la Grand’Cour describes hand-harvested whole bunches placed uncrushed and undestemmed into low-temperature tanks saturated with carbon dioxide, followed by spontaneous fermentation to pressing without added sulfite or oenological products except intervention if a problem occurs.
Domaine de la Grand’Cour publishes its production base at 156 route de la Grand’Cour, Fleurie; CARTA geocodes that address as a point and does not use it as vineyard geometry.

Domaine de la Tournelle publishes its domaine base at 5 Petite Place in Arbois.

Domaine de la Tournelle Fleur de Savagnin is a distinct persistent wine from Domaine Labet's same-named wine; the producer describes it as 100% Savagnin from grey marl and deliberately ouillé/non-oxidative.

Ecocert currently lists Fabrice Dodane / Domaine de Saint-Pierre in Mathenay under EU organic agriculture certification.

Château Renard is a recurring white Arbois bottling of Domaine de Saint Pierre / Fabrice Dodane. Available vintage records show that its detailed composition should be temporalized rather than treated as permanently 100% Chardonnay.

claims.statement: Domaine des Terres Dorées is based in Charnay and maintains vineyard activity in the southern Beaujolais area and in several crus; CARTA retains the current source’s acreage arithmetic as unresolved rather than manufacturing a corrected total.

The current Rhône Tourisme listing places Domaine des Terres Dorées in Charnay and describes nine hectares of Chardonnay within the 37 hectares it attributes to the area around the estate, giving minority Beaujolais Chardonnay a specific southern producer route without resolving the source's separate total-area conflict.
Domaine des Terres Dorées is shown at its current public address, 565 route d’Alix, Charnay; the point represents the production/business base, not vineyard holdings.

From the 2024 harvest, Jean-Paul Brun entrusted operation and development of Domaine des Terres Dorées to Domaines Roger Zannier, while the announcement says Brun would remain involved in a five-year transition focused on making the wines.

claims.statement: The estate records Stéphane Robert creating Domaine du Tunnel in 1994 with 2.5 hectares, working Cornas, Saint-Péray and Saint-Joseph and adding Condrieu in 2013, reaching about twelve hectares, and taking its name from a 170-metre early-twentieth-century railway tunnel it rehabilitated at the lieu-dit Barras in Saint-Péray.

The Rare Wine Co. records Franck Balthazar leaving a textile factory in 2002 to take up Cornas, acquiring a planting of Petite Syrah in the Chaillot vineyard from Noël Verset alongside half-century-old family vines in Mazards and La Côte, ploughing with a horse, and fermenting whole-cluster with native yeasts in concrete before neutral demi-muids.

The estate's own chronology has Francis Vernay creating the domaine at Condrieu and planting its first vines at the Coteau de Vernon, releasing a first Coteau de Vernon cuvée in 1940; Georges Vernay taking over from his father in 1953; and Christine Vernay taking over in 1996, adding Terrasses de l'Empire and the estate's first red cuvées.

The Condrieu growers' organisation records Christine Vernay finishing the reconstruction of the Coteau de Vernon and converting the whole domaine to organic growing, across a range that spans the Côte-Rôtie, Condrieu and Saint-Joseph appellations, with the oldest vines dating to the hectare of Viognier Francis Vernay planted on the Coteau de Vernon in the 1930s.

The Syndicat des Vignerons de l'AOC Condrieu describes Georges Vernay as a man of vision and conviction who "worked hard to rebuild the hillsides and rescue the Viognier grape variety from obscurity", earning the nickname of the Pope of Condrieu. His own estate says he is globally recognised as having saved the abandoned variety and that he replanted his land and revitalised a generation of growers.

claims.statement: The Rare Wine Co. places Gonon, with Gripa and Chave, among the last old-school Saint-Joseph growers based in the original appellation around Tournon, Mauves and Saint-Jean-de-Muzols, records the brothers buying Raymond Trollat's 1915 planting on his retirement, and describes Marsanne planted by their father at the Coteau des Oliviers in 1958 and Roussanne in 1974.

The brothers are described as working organically, ploughing the steep slopes by horse, replanting by sélection massale from their own old vines, fermenting reds up to three weeks whole-cluster in open wooden vats and ageing in old 600-litre foudres.

The Rare Wine Co. records the Jamet brothers taking charge of the family domaine when their father Joseph retired in the mid-1980s, farming twenty-five plots across seventeen lieux-dits, and choosing each year which of those sites enter the flagship wine, with mostly whole-cluster fermentation and about 20% new wood.

The Rare Wine Co. records Chave making Hermitage since 1481, the current generation being father Gérard and son Jean-Louis, and the flagship red being assembled from the domaine's several Hermitage sites — "Bessards is our essential climat; you can't make a Grand Hermitage without it" — with the blend rebuilt from zero each year. The domaine also makes a Saint-Joseph rouge from vines in the historic centre of that appellation.
Domaine Labet is a family wine estate based in Rotalier in the southern Jura / Sud-Revermont; the Jura interprofessional profile documents 13.5 hectares across 45 parcels in four communes.
The Jura interprofessional profile identifies Alain, Julien, Charline and Romain Labet among the family vignerons of Domaine Labet.
The commune of Rotalier lists Domaine Labet at 14 Montée des Tilleuls, consistent with the Jura interprofessional profile's identification of the estate as based in Rotalier.

For the 2022 La Bardette Chardonnay, specialist retail/importer notes describe a 0.5-hectare west-facing La Bardette parcel planted in 1947 and more than 30 months of aging in used 228-litre barrels; the estate's broader La Bardette holdings include plantings of other ages, so this detail is scoped to the 2022 single-parcel bottling.
Domaine Labet's Fleur de Savagnin is documented as a Savagnin blend assembled from multiple Lias-marl parcels rather than a single vineyard wine; the listed plantings span multiple years and sites.

The Jura interprofessional profile describes La Cuvée du Hasard as Chardonnay from vines older than 60 years, blended from different Lias-marl terroirs and aged sous voile in old 228-litre pièces for 36 to 48 months.

claims.statement: Skurnik records a sixth-generation family estate at Gervans, Laurent Fayolle taking control in 2002 when his father and uncle divided the family domaine among their children, and seven hectares of parcels — many over sixty years old — in the granite hills behind the hill of Hermitage, across Crozes-Hermitage, Hermitage and Saint-Péray.
Domaine Marcel Lapierre is a family wine estate in Villié-Morgon created in 1909; its current estate page describes 18 hectares planted to Gamay noir à jus blanc, mainly in Morgon.
Domaine Lapierre states that all plots have been worked according to organic principles since the 1980s and that the vines have been Ecocert-certified since 2004.

Domaine Lapierre currently describes hand harvest, semi-carbonic maceration, indigenous yeasts, used-barrel completion and aging for Morgon, no filtration, and selective sulfur use; some export batches receive a light sulfur dose while bottles marked N are bottled without sulfur.
Domaine Marcel Lapierre is shown at its first-party address, 588 rue Rabelais, Villié-Morgon; the point represents the domaine base, not its Morgon or Beaujolais vineyard parcels.
Mathieu Lapierre joined the domaine in 2004, Camille Lapierre joined in 2013, and the siblings currently co-own and operate the family winery.
Domaine Marcel Lapierre produces a recurring Morgon bottling from Gamay; CARTA treats the named bottling as one durable wine identity across vintages.

Jules Chauvet was a technically engaged Beaujolais wine merchant, researcher and transmission figure; a 1963 co-authored paper documents his research on malic and lactic acid evolution during carbonic maceration, while Lapierre’s first-party history documents his later guidance to Marcel Lapierre.
Domaine Marcel Lapierre states that Marcel Lapierre was born in 1950, took over the family business in 1973, and died after the 2010 harvest in October 2010.

The domaine states that in 1981, under Jules Chauvet's guidance, Marcel Lapierre decided to vinify without added sulfur and shifted toward organic cultivation without chemical fertilizers or weedkillers.

claims.statement: The Rare Wine Co. records Noël Verset working Chaillots, Sabarotte and Champelrose, beginning to divest his vines in the late 1980s, selling his largest parcel in 2001 as he neared ninety, and making wine under his own name until 2006. Reynard vines went to Thierry Allemand, Sabarotte to Clape and Courbis, and a half hectare in Chaillots planted in 1912 to his nephew Franck Balthazar.
Verset's method is recorded as fully ripe low-yield fruit, no destemming, crushing by foot, fifteen to eighteen days in small concrete vats and basket pressing.

The Rare Wine Co. records the Michel family growing in Cornas for more than four hundred years, Robert's father Joseph as a pioneer of domaine-bottled Cornas in 1956, Robert taking over the family holding in 1975 at twenty-nine, and the vineyard growing from the 1.5 hectares his father farmed to about eight by the time he retired after the 2006 vintage.

Michel's wines came from Chaillot, Reynard and Tézier for the Cuvée des Coteaux and from La Geynale, described as a prized sub-cru high on the Reynard slope planted by his grandfather in 1910. He fermented long and whole-cluster for La Geynale and destemmed part of the Chaillot fruit, ageing in neutral demi-muids and pièces.

Polaner Selections records that Vincent Paris's uncle is Robert Michel, that his first vintage was 1997, that he made his first two wines with his uncle before renting facilities of his own, that he inherited most of his vines from his grandfather, and that he rented and then purchased vines from his uncle including Geynale in the Cornas amphitheatre.

The Condrieu growers' organisation records Yves Cuilleron taking over the family domaine in 1987 when it held 3.5 hectares in Condrieu and Saint-Joseph, and the estate reaching ninety hectares across six Northern Rhône AOCs plus IGP and Vin de France wines.

claims.statement: Maison Guigal records its founding by Etienne Guigal at Ampuis in 1946, Marcel Guigal taking over management in 1961 when his father lost his sight, Philippe Guigal joining as winemaker in 1997, a run of acquisitions including Vidal-Fleury, Château d'Ampuis, Jean-Louis Grippat, de Vallouit and Domaine de Bonserine, and its own cooperage from 2003. Scale, négoce and acquisition are part of this corridor's real ecology.
Guillaume Gilles is an independent vigneron based in Cornas; specialist sources document his own domaine from 2007 and the Cornas producer association lists him at 1 Grande Rue, Cornas.

Rosenthal Wine Merchant records that when Robert Michel retired after the 2006 vintage he "leased his prime parcel in the Chaillot vineyard" to Guillaume Gilles and "provided his cave" for Gilles's use. A lease is a tenure arrangement, not a sale: CARTA records farming and use, and asserts no transfer of ownership of either the parcel or the cellar.

Vine Trail reports that Guillaume Gilles became certified organic from 2020 and describes hand vineyard work, whole-bunch red fermentation, native yeasts, no fining or filtration, and restrained sulfur use.

Rosenthal describes Gilles eschewing the destemmer in virtually all cases, working the vineyards by hand, using the grapes' own yeasts, ageing in old demi-muids and bottling without fining or filtration. These are concrete practices attributed to a producer, not a movement identity.

Guillaume Gilles Les Peyrouses Rouge is a Syrah wine bottled as Côtes du Rhône, from an old-vines parcel on the flats in the commune of Cornas; Rosenthal describes the site's soils as sand and clay overlain with large galet stones.

claims.statement: Vine Trail identifies Cornas vigneron Marcel Juge as Guillaume Gilles's grandfather and describes Juge as an early personal reference point for Gilles's desire to work in wine.
After working with Robert Michel through 2006, Guillaume Gilles completed a stint with Jean-Louis Chave in Hermitage before starting independently in 2007.

Robert Michel mentored Guillaume Gilles; Vine Trail says Michel offered Gilles an apprenticeship in 2000 and that Gilles worked with him until Michel's 2006 retirement, while Rosenthal explicitly calls Gilles Michel's protégé.

claims.statement: Beattie & Roberts reports roughly one hectare of Garay's own vines in Saint-Étienne-de-Baïgorry just outside Irouléguy, another roughly one hectare near Orthez, and additional purchased fruit from Madiran and Spanish sites; owned/farmed vines and purchased fruit must remain distinct in CARTA.
Current importer documentation describes Imanol Garay as farming biodynamically and vinifying with native fermentations and very low-intervention cellar practice across his French and Spanish work.
Current importer documentation describes Garay using a mixed cellar of barrels, tanks and amphorae rather than one fixed vessel regime.
The 2023 Ixilune description differs materially from earlier documented vintages, reinforcing that Ixilune's grape composition and cellar treatment are vintage-specific rather than a timeless recipe.

Imanol Garay's Ixilune has been documented in different vintages as a blend centered on Raffiat de Moncade with Petit Manseng and Petit Courbu, and sometimes Gros Manseng; blend proportions and maceration vary by vintage.
Beattie & Roberts documents Clandestinus 2022 as one of Imanol Garay's representative wines, providing a distinct reference point from his white cuvées.
Beattie & Roberts documents La Altannativa 2021 as a Garay wine made from purchased Madiran Tannat, making it a useful anchor for distinguishing estate vines from purchased-fruit work.

Hegan Egin is a collaboration among Alfredo Egia, Imanol Garay, and Gile Iturriondobeitia, with Garay contributing low-intervention know-how, Gile working as winemaker, and Egia as viticulturist in Egia's 2022 account.
Multiple trade sources report that Imanol Garay worked with Richard Leroy before establishing his own project.

claims.statement: The same source records that Stéphan has added no sulfites since 1997, ferments with indigenous yeasts using carbonic maceration, ages in old barrels and neither fines nor filters, with his largest plot on the granite and gneiss terraces of Bassenon and replanting by massale selection of Sérine. Trade sources describe this work as natural; no self-description was captured.

iDealwine records that Jean-Michel Stéphan established his domaine at Tupin-Semons in Côte-Rôtie in 1991 after working at Domaine des Terres Dorées, Jean-Paul Brun's estate in Beaujolais — a documented professional route between two CARTA worlds.

The house dates itself to the 1808 creation of Calvet et Compagnie in the rue de l'Hermitage at Tain, records Michel Chapoutier creating the first plot selections — Sélections Parcellaires — in 1989, and his taking control in 1990 and beginning to apply biodynamic cultivation.

claims.statement: Louis/Dressner describes a house label code in which most regular Overnoy cuvées share the same front label: wax color distinguishes Chardonnay, Savagnin and Ploussard, 50 cl identifies topped Savagnin in the profile, and bottling dates added since 2018 help distinguish separate releases of one vintage.

claims.statement: Louis/Dressner states that its United States allocation of Overnoy is fewer than 400 bottles a year for the whole country. CARTA treats that as dated importer-market context: scarcity explains access pressure but does not prove quality or educational value.

The French public business register lists GAEC Emmanuel Houillon Overnoy as an active grape-growing business based in Pupillin; Louis/Dressner identifies the wine estate as Emmanuel Houillon / Maison Pierre Overnoy.
Louis/Dressner's current estate profile lists Chardonnay, Savagnin, Ploussard and Trousseau among the grapes grown by Emmanuel Houillon / Maison Pierre Overnoy.

claims.statement: Louis/Dressner reports that Pierre Overnoy took over the family's vineyard portion in Pupillin in 1968, later trained and worked with Emmanuel Houillon, and retired in 2001 while remaining present around the family and estate.

claims.statement: Louis/Dressner's profile and Emmanuel Houillon interview document Houillon beginning his apprenticeship with Pierre Overnoy in 1990, returning full-time in 1997, and taking over the estate in 2001 after years of working and learning alongside Overnoy.

claims.statement: The house records its founding in 1834 by Antoine Jaboulet on the hill of l'Hermitage at Tain, the creation of Hermitage La Chapelle in 1961, Gérard Jaboulet taking up the torch from 1977 until his death in 1997, and Caroline Frey assuming control in 2006 and beginning the conversion to organic and biodynamic farming. A historic house identity survived a change of owning family.

claims.statement: Souhaut's importer describes whole-bunch fermentation with no destemming, spontaneous fermentation without added yeast, gentle hand punch-downs rather than heavy pumping over, and sulfur limited to about 25 mg/L. This is an importer's description of practice, not the producer's own account of an identity.

Hervé Souhaut created Domaine Romaneaux-Destezet with Béatrice Souhaut in 1993, based at Arlebosc in the Ardèche hills above Saint-Joseph. The estate's range includes Saint-Joseph Syrah alongside Vallée du Doux wines: the producer's base sits outside the Saint-Joseph geography, and the base point must never be read as the location of the Saint-Joseph vines.

location.description: Hervé Souhaut's estate base is at Arlebosc in the northern Ardèche, in the hills above Saint-Joseph and outside that appellation's geography. The base is not the location of the Saint-Joseph vines, and no coordinate is asserted.

claims.statement: Allemand is described as using as little sulfur as possible, ageing eighteen months to two years on lees without racking, and having released a Sans Soufre bottling in only five vintages seen by his importer: 1998, 1999, 2001, 2004 and 2011. Low sulfur here is a practice inside a source-described traditional framework, not a movement label.

The same importer that documents Allemand's work with the elder Cornas growers states plainly that he "is a disciple of no one's" and describes his approach as uniquely his while deeply rooted in the past. Working for someone is not being mentored by them.

The Rare Wine Co. records that Thierry Allemand worked during the day for Joseph Michel and then for Michel's son Robert, while working nights helping Noël Verset, and that Verset later sold him some of his Reynard vines dating to the beginning of the twentieth century.

The Condrieu growers' organisation records that Yves Cuilleron, Pierre Gaillard and François Villard began the project in 1996 to revive the old Seyssuel vineyard north of Vienne, producing a first vintage in 1998, and that the project farms twelve hectares of Seyssuel hillside planted to Syrah and Viognier.

Sotanum, with Héluicum and Taburnum, is sold as an IGP Collines Rhodaniennes wine. Seyssuel's slopes sit in the same corridor as the crus and are farmed by three cru producers, and the wine is still not a cru wine, because no cru appellation covers that ground.

claims.statement: Soleras del Pacífico is Jake Neustadt's project, begun from the opportunity in 2017 to work with old Palomino vines at Evangelho Vineyard while he was working as a Bedrock Wine Co. viticulturist.

Evangelho Vineyard in Contra Costa County was planted in the 1890s on deep sandy soils; Soleras del Pacífico documents just over 100 Palomino vines there, while Bedrock identifies itself as the vineyard owner and farmer.

The Flor of Evangelho is documented as a single-vineyard Palomino Fino wine in a fino-style solera established in 2017: native barrel fermentation is followed by light spring fortification to favor flor, fractional blending through a four-level solera, maturation under flor and unfiltered bottling.

location.description: Specialist importer sources place Chaillot among the named Cornas sites worked successively by Robert Michel, Noël Verset, Guillaume Gilles and Franck Balthazar. CARTA holds no parcel geometry and does not treat the name as one undivided holding.

The estate and the Condrieu growers' organisation place the Coteau de Vernon as the site of Francis Vernay's foundational hectare of Viognier and of the terrace reconstruction Christine Vernay completed. No parcel geometry is asserted.

location.description: The Rare Wine Co. describes La Geynale as a prized sub-cru high on the Reynard slope, planted by Robert Michel's grandfather in 1910; Polaner records vines there passing from Michel to his nephew Vincent Paris. No parcel geometry is asserted.

Rosenthal describes Les Peyrouses as an old-vines parcel on the flats in the commune of Cornas, while the wine is Côtes du Rhône Rouge. INAO separately defines the Cornas AOP as a delimited area within the sole commune. Sacred Thirst documents whole-cluster native-yeast fermentation in concrete tanks, basket pressing, transfer by gravity into 500-liter barrels with up to one-third new oak depending on vintage, and about 18 months of élevage before unfined, unfiltered bottling.

Château Renard is a recurring white Arbois bottling of Domaine de Saint Pierre / Fabrice Dodane. Available vintage records show that its detailed composition should be temporalized rather than treated as permanently 100% Chardonnay.
